name: inputs-pane-resets-a-shortcut
description:
A row put back on the chord Atrium ships: the shipped chord acts again and the rebound one stops, in the same run, and the file stops naming the action.

The Inputs pane could rebind a shortcut and clear it, but nothing put the default back. A user who had moved toggleSidebar off cmd+s had no way to say 'never mind' short of hand-editing hotkeys.json, and hand-editing it wrote the default in as a user value - which is the thing that must not happen. An action the file names is pinned: a change to what Atrium ships never reaches that profile again. So the reset REMOVES the entry rather than writing cmd+s into it, and that is what the actions:{} assertion below measures.

toggleSidebar is the action under test for the same reason inputs-pane-rebinds-a-shortcut picked it: collapsing the sidebar is the only effect readable from one window, and that scenario already measured the pixel deltas this one reuses. The fixture stages cmd+shift+j, so the row starts AWAY from its shipped chord - which is also what makes the reset control appear at all.

THE CONTROL'S ABSENCE IS HALF THE PROOF. openCommandBar is not in the fixture, so it arrives at its shipped cmd+t and must carry no reset button. A pane that offered one on every row would pass the positive leg on its own.

THE LIVE-RELOAD LEG IS THE SAME SHAPE inputs-pane-rebinds-a-shortcut uses, run the other way: cmd+shift+j must stop acting and cmd+s must start, both without a relaunch, which is only true if OnHotkeysSaved re-seeded NativeHotkeyMap from what the reset wrote. Note that cmd+s does NOT reach Save Page here - the reset re-bound it to toggleSidebar, so Atrium claims it before the stock command sees it.
